id: bounded-dimension-bounded-exponent-finiteness-proof
kind: route
title: Bounded-dimension separated microstates of a bounded-exponent group converge to a faithful linear representation
target: bounded-dimension-microstates-bounded-exponent-group-is-finite
requires: []
---

**Proof.** Let `G` have exponent `N`, generated by a finite symmetric set `S`
(closed under inverses), and let `c`, `D` be as in the claim. Write `B_k` for
the ball of radius `k` in the word metric of `S`, and `|| . ||_2`,
`|| . ||_op` for the normalized Hilbert--Schmidt and operator norms on `M_d`.
Both norms are invariant under left and right multiplication by unitaries. In
a fixed dimension `d`,

```text
||X||_op <= sqrt(d) ||X||_2.                                      (P1)
```

**Step 1: one dimension.** For each `k` choose `rho_k : B_k -> U(d_k)` with
`d_k <= D`, defect `eps_k = 1/k` in `(BE1)` and separation `c` in `(BE2)`.
Some `d <= D` occurs for infinitely many `k`; pass to that subsequence.

**Step 2: a limit tuple.** The tuples `(rho_k(s))_(s in S)` lie in the compact
set `U(d)^S`. Pass to a further subsequence converging to `(u_s)_(s in S)`.
Let `F(S)` be the free group on the letters of `S` and define
`rho : F(S) -> U(d)` by `s -> u_s`.

**Step 3: the limit is multiplicative on words.** Fix a word `w = t_1 ... t_L`
with letters `t_j in S` and value `g` in `G`, and let `p_j` be the value of
`t_1 ... t_j`. For `k >= L` all `p_j` lie in `B_k`, and `(BE1)` gives
`||rho_k(p_(j-1)) rho_k(t_j) - rho_k(p_j)||_2 < 1/k`. Multiplying by unitaries
does not change the norm, so telescoping over `j` gives

```text
||rho_k(g) - rho_k(t_1) rho_k(t_2) ... rho_k(t_L)||_2 <= L / k.
```

By `(P1)` the same bound holds in operator norm up to the factor `sqrt(d)`.
Matrix multiplication is continuous, so `rho_k(t_1) ... rho_k(t_L) -> rho(w)`
and hence `rho_k(g) -> rho(w)`. So `rho(w)` depends only on `g`: two words
with the same value have the same limit of `rho_k(g)`. Therefore `rho`
factors through a homomorphism `rho : G -> U(d)`; in particular
`u_(s^(-1)) = u_s^*`, because `s s^(-1)` has value `1` and `rho(1) = I` by Step 4.

**Step 4: faithfulness.** Let `g != 1` in `G`. For large `k` both `g` and `1`
lie in `B_k`. By `(BE1)`, `||rho_k(1) - I||_2 <= ||rho_k(1) rho_k(1) - rho_k(1)||_2 < eps_k`,
since `rho_k(1)` is unitary. So `(BE2)` gives
`||rho_k(g) - I||_2 >= c - eps_k`. Passing to the limit,
`||rho(g) - I||_2 >= c > 0`, so `rho(g) != I`. Hence `rho` is injective.

**Step 5: finiteness.** `rho(G)` is a finitely generated subgroup of
`U(d) <= GL_d(C)`, and every element has order dividing `N`. By Schur's
theorem it is finite, and `G` is isomorphic to it.  **QED**

**Scope.** Only finite generation, finite exponent (in fact periodicity is
enough for Step 5) and the uniform bounds `c`, `D` are used. The dimension
cap is essential: with `d_k -> infinity`, `(P1)` gives no operator-norm
control and Step 3 fails, which is exactly the regime a counterexample to
`hyperlinear-fg-bounded-exponent-groups-are-finite` must occupy.
